hints.title: Keep the zero case before cancelling
hints.body: From ab=ac, rearrange to a(b−c)=0. This means a=0 or b=c, with both also allowed.
hints.recap: A product equal to zero forces at least one zero factor.
hints.pitfall: You may not divide by a unless it is known to be nonzero.
hints.pause: Compare this OR statement with each individual claim.

recall.reminder: A product equal to zero forces at least one zero factor.

hints.title: Test the nonzero branch
hints.body: In the branch where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> is nonzero, determine the relation between <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></math>. Choose permitted values to test statements I and II.
hints.recap: A counterexample must still satisfy the given equation.
hints.pitfall: A possible value is not a necessary value.
hints.pause: Record which claims survive this branch.

hints.title: Test the zero branch
hints.body: Now set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>. Work out what restrictions the original equation then places on <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></math>.
hints.recap: Zero factors can remove restrictions on the other factors.
hints.pitfall: Do not cancel a factor that may be zero.
hints.pause: Choose values in this branch and decide whether any remaining claim must hold.

recall.reminder: Zero factors can remove restrictions on the other factors.

solution:
1. Factor the premise. a(b−c)=0 gives a=0 or b=c.

2. Reject I and II. a=b=c=1 satisfies the premise, yet a≠0 and neither b nor c is zero.

3. Reject III. a=0,b=1,c=2 also satisfies the premise, but b≠c.

Answer A: none of them. At least one of two alternatives must hold; that does not identify a particular one that always holds.
knowledgePattern: Distinguish a zero-product disjunction from its individual alternatives
